title: Right Hop Converter
context: Grade 5, the pages on converting bigger units into smaller ones. An adult sees zeros being added. What the pages are doing is the same count of places as before, run the other way: each place to the right multiplies the number by 10, and the zeros that appear are places held open.

writeup.why: Change a measure from a bigger unit to a smaller one by counting the places from the unit you have to the unit you want and multiplying the number by 10 for each, change a mixed measure bigger part first, keep the zeros that hold places, and write a long road in metres.
writeup.look: One row of the unit chart with digit tiles in its columns, two pins, a point that hops right, and grey zeros dropping into empty columns.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Right Hop Converter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of hops the point has made. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. One row of the chart runs across the middle of the area at y 380: seven columns, each 140 wide, from x 90 to x 1070, headed kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle and the unit names violet, labelled Unit. The given measure stands in deep blue digit tiles, labelled Given, with the point in the gap after its unit. The deep blue have pin stands over the unit you have at y 300, and the green want pin is dragged along the same line. The Hop button stands at x 900, y 230, and each hop moves the point one gap to the right and draws a vermilion arrow under the row along y 470, labelled Move, multiply the number by 10. Each column the point passes that holds no digit gets a grey zero, labelled Place holder. On the second and third phases the smaller part's card waits at x 120, y 560 with the Add part button beside it at x 400, y 560, and the column being filled is amber. On the fourth phase the road sign hangs above the row at x 120, y 220, and a second sign appears beside it once the answer is in. The answer is read in green, labelled Answer, at x 120, y 660, with its unit. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a comma key for grouping and a delete key. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. The measure the question gives, in the unit it is given in, is deep blue, labelled Given or Measure. The measure the working reaches, and a reading on a scale, is green, labelled Answer, Reading or Same measure. The places moved across the unit chart, and the worth of one small mark on a scale, are vermilion, labelled Move or One mark. A unit fact, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet, labelled Unit fact, Unit or Other scale. The part taken away, and a part left over after sharing, are rose, labelled Taken away or Left over. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open inside a number, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. Rulers, tapes, jugs, scales, thermometer tubes, chart lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last measure stays on the row with its hops drawn beneath, its zeros in place and its answer in green with its unit.

phases.win: two grey zeros drop in behind the digit, and the grams turn green
phases.does: drags the want pin to g, counts the places, and hops the point right once for each
phases.goal: count the places from the unit you have to the unit you want; each place to the right multiplies the number by 10
phases.says: Pin the unit you want. Hop right once for each place.
phases.check: Away from the screen: from metres to centimetres, which way do you go, and how many places?
phases.feels: the point sliding right and zeros dropping in behind the digit
phases.hands: On the paper chart, write a weight in hectograms under hg. Put a coin on hg and another on g, count the steps, and move the paper point one column right for each, writing a zero in every column it passes.
phases.tries: First rung: count the places between the pins without hopping. Second rung: hop once and read the measure. Third rung: the same task between two neighbouring units, before the question's own measure returns.

wrong.move: hops the point to the left instead of the right
wrong.screen: the point stays and the measure is read back in the unit it now sits after, far less than the card shows; the pins light amber and the places between them are counted again one hop at a time

wrong.why: zeros look like nothing, so they seem safe to leave off
wrong.move: types the digit and stops, with no zeros after it
wrong.screen: the columns the point passed are lit amber inside the answer, one at a time, each waiting for its grey zero

phases.win: a grey zero drops into the empty hundreds column, and the answer turns green

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, as the third hop lands, three grey zeros drop in one after another like counters, and the second road sign swings down beside the first with the length in metres.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet hopped. On the first phase a weight in hectograms sits in the row with the have pin on hectograms and the want pin loose. On the second a capacity's litres part sits in the row and its millilitres part waits on a card beside it. On the third a length's kilometres part sits in the row and its metres part, only two digits long, waits on a card. On the fourth the length row lies under a road sign that reads the road's length in kilometres, with the word over before it. One thing moves, once: the want pin gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any measure set on any row, pinned and hopped right to any smaller unit, with mixed measures added part by part. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on places to the right, mixed measures in the smaller unit, zeros that hold places, and the road.

observations.why: a smaller unit needs more of itself to make the same measure.
observations.soWhat: moving to a smaller unit multiplies the number by 10 for each place.
observations.observe: Each hop to the right made the number bigger, but the measure on the card stayed the same.

observations.why: each column the point passes is one unit of the chart, and it must hold a digit.
observations.soWhat: the zeros are part of the answer, not decoration.
observations.observe: Grey zeros dropped in behind the digits as the point hopped past empty columns.

observations.why: the two parts are in different units until the bigger part is changed.
observations.soWhat: change the bigger part first, then add the smaller part.
observations.observe: The litres part hopped first, and only then did the millilitres slide in beside it.

observations.why: changing the unit changes the number, not what we know about the road.
observations.soWhat: a word like over or about stays with the measure in any unit.
observations.observe: The second road sign still read over.

source_tool.description: One row of the unit chart runs across the working area, seven columns from kilo to milli with violet unit names, labelled Unit. The given measure is set in deep blue digit tiles, labelled Given, one digit to a column, with the point after its unit. A deep blue pin stands on the unit you have, and a green pin is dragged to the unit you want. The Hop button moves the point one column to the right; each hop draws a vermilion arrow under the row, labelled Move, multiply the number by 10, and the running count at the top left of the canvas counts the hops. Each column the point passes that holds no digit gets a grey zero, labelled Place holder. On the second and third phases a mixed measure is changed bigger part first, and the smaller part then slides into its own columns, the column being filled lit amber. On the last phase the row is the length row, with a road sign reading over 4112 km. The answer is read in green, labelled Answer, with its unit.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a unit chart of seven columns from kilo to milli with the base unit in the middle, rulers and tapes marked in their units, kitchen scales, measuring jugs marked in millilitres, and thermometers with labelled marks.
Every measure is written with its unit on every line, and every decimal names the unit it is in, so 3.04 L is never shown as a bare 3.04.
Every mixed measure shown is ordinary: its smaller part is less than one of the larger unit.
Places are counted from the unit the child has to the unit the child wants, one hop at a time, and each hop shows the number, not the unit, divided or multiplied by 10.
Multiplying and dividing a measure happen in its smallest unit, in whole numbers, and a sharing that does not come out even shows what is left over.
A thermometer shows what one small mark is worth before its column is read, and a Celsius reading sits beside a Fahrenheit one only in the four pairs the chapter prints.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a hop across the chart, a carry across units, a length shared into equal pieces, or a column rising to a mark.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a unit or a mark the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the measure the question gives is deep blue, and the measure the working reaches, with a reading taken off a scale, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The places moved across the unit chart, each one dividing or multiplying the number by 10, and the worth of one small mark on a scale are vermilion. A unit fact such as 1 kg = 1000 g, the unit names on the chart and the other temperature scale are violet. The part taken away, and a remainder left over after sharing, are rose. The unit, column, mark or step being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Move, Unit fact, Taken away, Left over and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the places between the pins again. Is any column empty?
voice.onNext: A new measure. Pin the smaller unit you want.
voice.opening: A measure on the chart, and a pin on its unit.
voice.onFinish: You hopped right to a smaller unit and kept every place.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Set any measure and hop it anywhere to the right.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A mixed measure in the smaller unit
A zero that holds a place

placement.where: After the class has weighed kitchen packets and written each weight again in grams by counting places on their floor chart. The tool is what hops the point and drops each zero into place, which paper can only show finished.

answer_key.rule: Count the places from the unit you have to the unit you want. Each place to the right multiplies the number by 10, so one place multiplies by 10, two by 100 and three by 1000. For a mixed measure, change the bigger part into the smaller unit first, then add the smaller part. A zero holds any place inside the answer that has no digit. The road box prints no question, so the road question here is our own: NH44 is over 4112 km long, which is over 41,12,000 m.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's point and reads the measure back in that form, with the unit they named. The pins light amber beside it and the places between them are counted again one hop at a time. A missing zero is shown as an empty amber column inside the answer. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Count the places from the unit you have to the unit you want: from hg to g is two places to the right.
Each place to the right multiplies the number by 10, so multiply by 100.
items.question: A packet of tea weighs 4 hg. How many grams is that?
items.checkpoint: Count the places from the unit you have to the unit you want, and multiply the number by 10 for each place to the right.
items.misconception: Dividing instead of multiplying, which makes a packet of tea weigh less than a crumb.

steps: 1000 mL make 1 litre, so change the bigger part first: 4 litres is 4 x 1000 = 4000 mL.
Check: 4615 mL is still 4 whole litres and 615 mL more.
items.question: A bucket holds 4 L 615 mL. How many millilitres is that?
items.checkpoint: Change the bigger part into the smaller unit first, then add the smaller part.
items.misconception: Changing only the litres and forgetting to add the 615 mL, which leaves a bucket short.

steps: Change the kilometres first: 8 km is 8000 m.
The 0 in the hundreds place holds that place open.
items.question: A trail is 8 km 70 m long. How many metres is that?
items.checkpoint: A zero holds a place open inside the answer.
items.misconception: Writing the digits side by side and leaving out the zero, which reads as eight hundred seventy metres, far too short.

steps: Count the places from km to m: three places to the right.
Each place to the right multiplies the number by 10, so multiply by 1000.
NH44 is over 4112 km long, so it is over 41,12,000 m long.
items.question: This is our own question, because the road box prints no question. NH44 is over 4112 km long. Over how many metres is that?
items.checkpoint: Keep the word over: the road is longer than the number says, in any unit.
items.misconception: Dropping the word over and saying the road is exactly that long.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many centimetres is 2 m 58 cm?
How many grams is 5 kg 8 g?
How many litres is 3 kL 260 L?
How many centimetres is 4 m 6 cm?
Another of our own questions: NH44 is over 4112 km long. Over how many decametres is that?

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Count the places from the unit you have to the unit you want, then multiply the number by 10 for each place to the right. Change the bigger part of a mixed measure first, then add the smaller part. Check every zero that holds a place open. The road box prints no question, so say plainly that the road question is our own, and keep the page's word over. Write litres in full before is or equals when a sentence is read aloud.
generation_prompt: Build a unit conversion tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, the twin of the left hop converter. One row of the unit chart, seven columns from kilo to milli with violet unit names, holds a measure as deep blue digit tiles with the point after its unit. A deep blue pin marks the unit you have and a green pin is dragged to the unit you want. A Hop button moves the point one column right and draws a vermilion arrow labelled Move, multiply the number by 10; each empty column the point passes gets a grey zero.
